title: Structuring a modern AI team — Denys Linkov, Wisedocs

primary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 74%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on human collaboration, team composition, and organizational design for AI teams rather than any specific technical AI subsystem. The advice is cross-domain with concrete examples drawn from enterprise AI team building and healthcare medical record processing at Wisedocs. The talk spans from initial AI adoption planning through ongoing production operations across two team-building experiences in 2021 and 2024. Content is accessible to managers and engineers without deep ML expertise, focusing on organizational strategy over technical depth. A structured conference presentation delivered at the AI Engineer series covering three themes across nine sections. All eleven evidence anchors are directly quoted from the transcript with grade 'said_in_transcript'.

summary: Denys Linkov opens by addressing the trend of companies declaring themselves 'AI first' and the resulting pressure on hiring managers. He frames the talk around three themes: the anatomy of an AI team, the evolution of a generalist, and hiring. He categorizes companies along a spectrum — technology companies, verticalized or services companies (like Palantir or Wisedocs), and tech-enabled companies — each facing different challenges: domain knowledge gaps, all-or-nothing dynamics, or tech capability gaps respectively. He argues technology is not the primary limiter, citing persistent fax markets, slow contactless payment adoption, and the 40-year digitization timeline for medical records. This leads to 'Ampere's Wager': would you trade your domain-knowledgeable team for five researchers from top labs? He also poses 'Blackwell's Wager': do you want GPUs or a team? He emphasizes AI teams must define use cases, integrate products, measure ROI, find data, build interfaces, and sell — no single role covers all. He urges leaders to identify their actual bottleneck before hiring. Linkov details building his first ML team in 2021 at a conversational AI company, hiring generalists balanced across model training, serving, and business acumen, writing a custom MLOps platform, and owning six microservices. In 2024, with advanced open source tools, some training shifted toward commercial APIs and prompt tuning, while domain knowledge requirements increased for medical record processing. He introduces inner loop (daily core activities) and outer loop (broader differentiating activities) frameworks, warning that a weak technical loop causes execution struggles and a weak domain loop prevents finding product-market fit. On upskilling, he says people need to learn to build, become domain experts, and be human-facing — moving from static PRDs to functional prototypes, having domain experts write use cases with LLM literacy, and putting engineers on customer calls. His team holds weekly 30-minute learning sessions. On hiring, he argues people are hired to hold context and act on context, that AI agents cannot fully replace human expertise and accountability, and that hiring should follow first principles rather than trends. He questions the trend against hiring junior engineers, citing YC's AI school. He calls for relevant interview questions over LeetCode-style problems. Three closing lessons: know what team you need to win, cross-functional teams will be built in different ways with greater overlap, and continuous learning is mandatory given how fast the field moves.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction to AI-First Mandates
sections.summary: Linkov introduces himself and the talk's three themes: anatomy of an AI team, evolution of a generalist, and hiring. He references companies like Shopify, Duolingo, and Zapier declaring AI-first strategies and the pressure this creates for hiring managers.

sections.title: Anatomy of an AI Team and Company Types
sections.summary: Categorizes companies as technology companies, verticalized/services companies, or tech-enabled companies. Each type faces different challenges — domain knowledge gaps, all-or-nothing dynamics, or tech capability gaps — and makes different buy-vs-build decisions accordingly.

sections.title: Technology as an Enabler, Not a Limiter
sections.summary: Argues that 90% of needed technology already exists, citing persistent fax markets, slow contactless payment adoption, and 40-year medical record digitization timeline. Team structure should reflect how technology is used, not the technology itself.

sections.title: Do You Need an AI Researcher? Ampere's Wager
sections.summary: Questions whether hiring AI researchers is necessary before hitting scale or specialty needs. Introduces 'Ampere's Wager': would you trade your domain-knowledgeable team for five top-lab researchers? Emphasizes that AI teams must handle use case definition, product integration, ROI measurement, data sourcing, interface building, and customer engagement.

sections.title: Identifying Your Bottleneck
sections.summary: Stresses identifying the actual bottleneck — shipping features, acquiring or retaining users, monetization, scalability, or reliability — before hiring. Warns against shipping your org chart and getting weird product behaviors from siloed teams.

sections.title: Building the First ML Team (2021)
sections.summary: Details building a generalist ML team at a conversational AI company with goals of serving hundreds of thousands of concurrent models, multi-domain support, low cost, and real-time training/serving. Prioritized model training, model serving, and business acumen. Built custom MLOps, fine-tuned encoder models, and owned six microservices.

sections.title: Building the Second AI Team (2024) and Inner/Outer Loops
sections.summary: Describes building a 2024 team with advanced open source tools, shifting toward commercial APIs, prompt tuning, and decoder/encoder models. Domain knowledge requirements increased for medical record processing. Introduces inner loop (daily core activities) and outer loop (broader differentiating activities) framework for team structure and reskilling.

sections.title: Feedback Loops, Generalists vs. Specialists, and Upskilling
sections.summary: Explains that a weak technical loop causes execution struggles and a weak domain loop prevents product-market fit. Generalists win early; specialists are needed only for the final 5% of performance. For upskilling, people need to learn to build, become domain experts, and be human-facing. Advocates moving from static PRDs to functional prototypes, having domain experts write use cases with LLM literacy, and putting engineers on customer calls. Describes weekly 30-minute team learning sessions.

sections.title: Hiring: Context, Trends, and First Principles
sections.summary: Argues people are hired to hold context and act on context; AI agents cannot fully replace human expertise and accountability. Hiring should follow first principles, not trends — questions the trend against junior engineers, citing YC's AI school for 2,000 young people. Calls for relevant interview questions over LeetCode-style problems.

sections.title: Revisiting Ampere's Wager and Final Lessons
sections.summary: Revisits Ampere's Wager, preferring domain-expert teams over top researchers for his company. Introduces Blackwell's Wager (GPUs or a team). Three closing lessons: know what team you need to win, cross-functional teams will be built differently with greater overlap, and continuous learning is mandatory given the speed of change.
